question: With what images does the poem describe Jerusalem at the very beginning, and what contrast appears between what she was and what she has become?
The verb נָחַם (nacham, “comfort”) returns several times in the phrase “there is no one to comfort her”: who seeks comfort, from whom, and why does this lack weigh so heavily in the poem?
The 22 verses begin, in Hebrew, with the letters of the alphabet in order: what can an acrostic express when the voice of Zion says “look and see if there is any sorrow like mine”?
The city weeps and at the same time says “I have been most rebellious”: how do you usually bring together pain and honesty about your own guilt when you pray?
What actions does the chapter attribute to the Lord against Zion, and with what comparisons is He described in verses 4 and 5?
What responsibility does the poem attribute to the prophets who announced “false and deceptive visions,” and how is this linked to the fall of the city?
The verb בָּלַע (bala‘, “swallow up, destroy”) appears in the mouth of the poet and in that of the enemies: what changes when the same word is spoken by different voices?
The poet says “pour out your heart like water in the presence of the Lord”: what place does sincere lament have in your life of prayer?
How does “the man who has seen affliction” describe what he suffered, and what images of siege, prison and attack does he use?
What brings about the turn of verse 21, and how do the statements about the Lord's loving devotion live alongside the pain of the previous verses?
The verb זָכַר (zakar, “remember”) links the plea to God and the memory of one's own soul: what role does remembrance have at the center of this poem, which is a triple acrostic of 66 verses?
“Let us examine and test our ways, and turn back to the LORD”: what concrete step could this invitation mean for you now?
What comparisons does the chapter use to show how the sons of Zion, the Nazirites and the mothers changed during the siege?
Why does the poem blame prophets and priests, and what irony is there in the leaders themselves being treated as “unclean”?
The verb שָׁפַךְ (shafakh, “pour out”) appears with stones, with God's wrath and with the blood of the righteous: what do these three scenes of pouring out suggest together?
The people hoped for help from “a nation that could not save”: in what things are you tempted to trust when you feel threatened?
What losses does the community list in its plea for the Lord to remember, and what groups of people are mentioned?
Verse 7 speaks of the sins of the fathers and verse 16 says “because we have sinned”: how does the poem deal with the guilt of different generations?
The phrase “from generation to generation” uses דּוֹר (dor, “generation”) for the Lord's throne: what contrast does it make with the people's situation described before?
This last chapter has 22 verses, but does not follow the alphabet: what does the book communicate by ending with a plea and a doubt, without an answer?
“Restore us to Yourself, O LORD, so that we may return”: what part of the change do you expect from God, and what part do you feel is yours?
